summary: Describes extensions to the IP architecture so hosts on switched data link subnetworks can make better use of the connections those networks offer. It relaxes assumptions about what counts as a local destination. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Today a host decides whether to send a packet straight to its neighbour or through a router by looking at IP addresses alone. This memo argues that decision should also consider the traffic itself, so a switched network can set up the kind of connection an application actually needs.

subtitle: Letting a host decide to send directly or through a router based on traffic, not on IP addresses alone.

tldr.problem: The IP model decides whether two hosts talk directly or through a router using only their IP addresses, which wastes the connections a switched network can set up on demand.
tldr.mechanism: The memo relaxes that rule. A host may connect straight to a peer on the same data link subnetwork, or take a shortcut past its first-hop router, whenever the quality of service or traffic needs of the application justify it.
tldr.outcome: The decision stops being tied to the addressing information, so groups of hosts and routers can be given their own address prefix and act as both first and last hop for their members.

today: RFC 1937 is an Informational memo from May 1996, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a model for switched virtual circuit subnetworks such as ATM, Frame Relay and X.25, and it names NHRP and ARP as the kinds of mechanism it assumes for address resolution rather than specifying one of its own.

sections.title: Background: The Local or Remote Decision
sections.content:
The IP architecture assumes that each data link subnetwork is labeled with a single IP subnet number. Hosts with the same subnet number communicate directly, with no routers involved, and hosts with different subnet numbers always communicate through one or more routers. As RFC 1620 notes, these assumptions may be too restrictive for large data networks, and specifically for networks built on switched virtual circuit (SVC) technologies such as ATM, Frame Relay and X.25, because they impose constraints on communication among hosts and routers through the network and may prevent full use of what the underlying subnetwork can offer.

The familiar model is restated here. An IP address of a host with an interface attached to a particular link is a tuple of prefix length, address prefix and host number, where the host number is unique within the subnet address prefix. When a host sends a packet, it must decide whether the destination address identifies an interface connected to one of the links the host is attached to. This is the local or remote decision, and its outcome is based on the destination address and on the address and prefix length associated with the local interfaces. If the outcome is local, the host resolves the IP address to a link layer address, for example with ARP, and sends the packet directly. If the outcome is remote, the host uses one of its first-hop routers and relies on IP routing.

So two attributes of the IP subnet model hold. Hosts with a common subnet address prefix are assumed to be attached to a common link, and they communicate with each other directly, without any routers, which is the local outcome. Hosts with different subnet address prefixes are assumed to be attached to different links, and they communicate with each other only through routers, which is the remote outcome. A typical example of applying the model to an SVC-based subnetwork is Classical IP and ARP over ATM, RFC 1577, which follows the traditional IP subnet model and introduces the notion of a Logical IP Subnetwork (LIS). The consequence is that a host must set up an ATM SVC to any host within its LIS, and must forward packets through a router for destinations outside it. The memo stresses that this decision is based solely on the information carried by the destination address and on the address and prefix lengths associated with the local interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The IP rules say that hosts sharing a subnet number talk directly and hosts with different subnet numbers talk through a router. The rule uses only the addresses, so it never takes the traffic into account.

sections.title: Motivations: Applications Do Not All Behave Alike
sections.content:
The diversity of TCP/IP applications produces a wide range of traffic characteristics. Some applications last a very short time and generate only a few packets between a pair of hosts, such as ping and DNS. Others have a short lifetime but generate a relatively large volume of packets, such as FTP. Some have a relatively long lifetime but generate relatively few packets, such as Telnet. The memo also anticipates applications with a relatively long lifetime and a large volume of packets, such as video-conferencing.

SVC-based data link subnetworks offer capabilities that other subnetworks, such as Ethernet and Token Ring, do not. Being able to set up and tear down SVCs dynamically lets communication resources such as bandwidth be dedicated and redistributed between the entities attached to the subnetwork. These capabilities do not come for free. The mechanisms that provide them carry overhead, such as the time needed to establish an SVC and the resources used to maintain state for it, and there may also be a monetary cost. The benefits therefore have to be weighed carefully against the overhead they introduce.

The key issue for using these subnetworks in a TCP/IP environment is SVC management, which includes establishing and tearing down circuits, specifying the class of service, and sharing circuits. At one end of the spectrum, an implementation could require SVC establishment between communicating entities on a common data link subnetwork for any application. At the other end, communicating entities could always go through a router, whatever the application. Given the range of applications, either extreme is likely to be a poor fit for making efficient use of what the data link layer provides.

The traditional IP subnet model is too restrictive for flexible and adaptive use of these subnetworks, because the use of a subnetwork is driven by information completely unrelated to the characteristics of the applications running over it. Under RFC 1577 the host must set up an SVC to any host within its LIS and route packets outside it through a router, so the forwarding decision and the SVC management are based solely on the addresses and the subnet mask, with no relation to the nature of the applications that generated the packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Different applications need different things. A name lookup is one packet each way; a file transfer is many packets; a video call is a long steady flow. A switched network can set up a connection to suit each one, but the IP rules hide that choice.

sections.title: A Decision Driven by Traffic
sections.content:
Consider a host attached to an SVC-based data link subnetwork, and assume the local or remote decision is not constrained by the IP subnet model. When such a host needs to send a packet, it could consider a best-effort SVC to the first hop router, an SVC to the first hop router dedicated to a particular type of service such as predictive real time, a dedicated SVC to the first hop router, a best-effort SVC to a router closer to the destination than the first hop router, an SVC to such a router dedicated to a particular type of service, a dedicated SVC to such a router, a best-effort SVC directly to the destination if it is on the same data link subnetwork, an SVC directly to the destination dedicated to a particular type of service, or a dedicated SVC directly to the destination.

Two observations follow. The forwarding decision at the host is more flexible than the local or remote decision of the IP subnet model. And the decision may take into account the quality of service and traffic requirements of the applications and the cost factors of establishing and maintaining a circuit, which improves the overall management of circuits. Removing the constraints imposed by the IP subnet model is therefore an important step towards better SVC management.

The memo then splits the decision in two. A source may have an SVC, dedicated or shared, to a destination if both the source and the destination are on a common data link subnetwork. The ability to create and use that SVC is completely decoupled from the source and destination IP addresses and is instead coupled to the quality of service and traffic characteristics of the application. In contrast with the IP subnet model, or the LIS mode, the local outcome becomes divorced from the addressing information.

A source may also go through one or more routers to reach a destination, either because the destination is not on the same data link subnetwork, or because it is on the same subnetwork but the quality of service and traffic requirements of the application do not justify a direct circuit. When the destination is elsewhere, the source may choose between its first-hop, or default, router and a shortcut to a router closer to the destination. When the destination is on the same subnetwork but a direct circuit is not justified, the source should still be able to go through a router. In both cases the choice is available regardless of the source and destination IP addresses, so the remote outcome and the choice between the two kinds of router become decoupled from the addressing information.
sections.plainLanguage: Under the relaxed rule, a host can pick the connection that suits the traffic: straight to the destination, to a router further along the way, or to its usual default router. The addresses stop deciding.

sections.title: What a Host Needs to Know to Connect Directly
sections.content:
The ability of a host to establish an SVC to a peer on a common switched data link subnetwork depends on its knowing the link layer address of the peer, or of an intermediate point closer to the destination. This document assumes that mechanisms exist to provide the host with that information. Some of the possible alternatives are NHRP, ARP, or static configuration, and other alternatives are not precluded.

Knowing the link layer address of the peer should not be taken as proof that the host and the peer can establish an SVC. The two may be on different data link subnetworks, and they may be on a common data link subnetwork that is partitioned.

One implication follows from a decision that depends on more than the addresses. A pair of hosts may simultaneously use two different means to reach each other, forwarding traffic for applications with different quality of service or traffic characteristics in different ways.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a host can talk directly to a neighbour it must know that neighbour's link layer address. And knowing the address is not enough, because the two may not be able to reach each other at all.

sections.title: Address Assignment and Local Addressing Groups
sections.content:
It is expected that if the total number of hosts and routers on a common SVC-based data link subnetwork is sufficiently large, then the hosts and routers could be partitioned into groups called Local Addressing Groups (LAGs). Each LAG would have hosts and routers, and the routers within a LAG would act as the first-hop routers for the hosts in that LAG. If the total number of hosts and routers is not large, then all of them could form a single LAG. The criteria for determining LAG sizes are outside the scope of this document.

To provide scalable routing, each LAG should be given an IP address prefix, and the elements within the LAG should be assigned addresses out of that prefix. The routers in a LAG would then advertise, through the appropriate routing protocols, routes to the prefix associated with the LAG. These routes would be advertised as directly reachable, with metric 0. The routers within a LAG would therefore act as the last-hop routers for the hosts within the LAG as well as their first hop.
sections.plainLanguage: A large switched network is split into groups. Each group gets its own block of IP addresses, and the routers inside the group are both the first stop for its hosts and the last stop for traffic bound for them.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
Different approaches to SVC-based data link subnetworks used by TCP/IP yield substantially different results in how well TCP/IP applications can exploit what the subnetworks provide. In the case of ATM, both LAN Emulation and Classical IP over ATM localize host changes below the IP layer, and may therefore be good first steps in an ATM deployment. On their own, though, these approaches are likely to be inadequate for full use of ATM.

The memo argues that any model which does not allow SVC management based on quality of service and traffic requirements will stand in the way of full use of SVC-based data link subnetworks. Enabling more direct connectivity for the applications that could benefit from the capabilities of these subnetworks, while relying on strict hop by hop paths for other applications, could make it easier to explore what the subnetworks can do. While the document does not define any specific coupling between quality of service, traffic characteristics and other parameters on the one hand and SVC management on the other, it stresses that standardization work in that area, so that an application could pass such parameters to influence SVC management through an appropriate API, is essential.

The proposed model uses the SVC-based infrastructure for the applications that could benefit from it and relies on a router-based overlay for everything else. That gives a balanced mix of router-based and switch-based infrastructure, with the balance set by the requirements of the applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo's advice is to let the applications that need a special connection have one, and to route everything else the ordinary way. It does not set out the rules in detail; it argues that others should work them out.
